notation.meaning: the arm or action selected at round t
how many times arm a was pulled before horizon n
the mean-reward gap between an optimal arm and arm a

algorithm.title: From an action trace to a gap sum

steps.title: Record the trace
steps.detail: Write the selected arm A_t at every round t.

steps.title: Count each arm
steps.detail: N_a(T) counts how often arm a appears before horizon T.

steps.title: Attach its gap
steps.detail: Every occurrence of arm a contributes the same model gap Δ_a.

steps.title: Regroup the sum
steps.detail: Replace the sum over time by one gap-times-count term per arm.

worked_example.title: Regroup one six-round action trace by arm
worked_example.intro: Take three arms with means 0.7, 0.5, and 0.6. Arm 1 is optimal. A short deterministic trace is enough to see the regret decomposition before any probability enters.

steps.title: Write the chronological actions
steps.detail: The order records what happened, but the pathwise pseudo-regret only needs how often each gap was paid.
steps.fallback: Across six rounds the selected arms are 1, 3, 2, 3, 3, and 1.

steps.title: Count each arm and compute its gap
steps.detail: Arm 1 is optimal, arm 2 is worse by 0.2, and arm 3 is worse by 0.1.
steps.fallback: The pull counts are 2, 1, and 3, while the corresponding gaps are 0, 0.2, and 0.1.

steps.title: Regroup time into gap times count
steps.detail: The two optimal-arm pulls cost zero; the single arm-2 pull and three arm-3 pulls contribute the entire value.
steps.fallback: The pathwise pseudo-regret is two times zero plus one times 0.2 plus three times 0.1, which equals 0.5.

worked_example.takeaway: The identity is deterministic bookkeeping: once an algorithm proof controls every suboptimal pull count, multiplying by gaps and summing gives pseudo-regret.
worked_example.boundary: This trace is an arithmetic illustration, not sampled data or an expected-regret experiment. The exact Lean theorem below uses rational model gaps and finite action traces.

source_theorem.label: Lemma 4.5 (regret decomposition)
source_theorem.fallback: Expected regret is the sum, over arms, of each gap times that arm's expected pull count.
source_theorem.plain: The standard stochastic-bandit decomposition converts control of suboptimal pull counts into expected regret.
source_theorem.relationship: BanditRLlib first proves the pathwise finite-trace identity. Algorithm chapters then integrate that bookkeeping identity under their own generated trajectory laws.

contract.model: Any stochastic bandit environment with a finite or countable action set, together with any policy and horizon n.
contract.assumptions: Arm means, action gaps, regret, and expected pull counts are defined; no concentration or algorithm-specific assumption is used.
contract.parameters: Horizon n, action gaps Δ_a, and pull counts T_a(n).
contract.regret: The textbook frequentist expected regret R_n.
contract.guarantee: An exact identity: regret equals the sum over actions of gap times expected pull count.

primary.title: Bandit Algorithms
primary.sections: Ch. 2, Ch. 3, and Ch. 5

notation.meaning: the sigma-algebra generated by the history observed through time t
conditional expectation given the information currently available
the total probability budget assigned to confidence failures

steps.title: Model conditional noise
steps.detail: State a conditional MGF or bounded-reward assumption on the generated history.

steps.title: Derive one tail bound
steps.detail: Convert the MGF bound into a deviation probability at a fixed index.

steps.title: Allocate confidence
steps.detail: Assign a finite, geometric, or telescoping share δ_i to every arm and time.

steps.title: Join the events
steps.detail: Use a union bound to obtain one good event consumed by an algorithm proof.

worked_example.title: Spend one confidence budget across six events
worked_example.intro: Suppose two arms are inspected at three checkpoints and the total allowed failure probability is delta = 0.05. The union-bound step is visible without hiding the accounting inside an algorithm.

steps.title: Name the six bad events
steps.detail: Each event says that one arm's empirical estimate misses its confidence radius at one checkpoint.
steps.fallback: There is one deviation event for each of two arms at each of three checkpoints, for six events in total.

steps.title: Give every event an explicit share
steps.detail: An equal schedule assigns delta divided by six to each fixed-index tail bound.
steps.fallback: Each event receives failure budget one over 120, and its fixed-index tail probability is bounded by that share.

steps.title: Join the events once
steps.detail: No independence is needed for the union bound; adding the six shares preserves the declared total budget.
steps.fallback: The chance that any of the six deviations occurs is at most the sum of their probabilities, which is 0.05.

worked_example.takeaway: A simultaneous good event is a budgeted collection of fixed-index facts. Finite, geometric, and telescoping schedules differ in how they distribute delta, not in the final union-bound logic.
worked_example.boundary: The event probabilities are illustrative inputs to the union bound. The compiled concentration declarations below specify the MGF, measurability, filtration, and index assumptions that justify each tail estimate.

source_theorem.label: Corollary 5.5 (sub-Gaussian tail)
source_theorem.fallback: A centered sub-Gaussian variable has an exponentially small upper-tail probability.
source_theorem.plain: The fixed-index tail estimate is the mathematical atom from which finite and all-time confidence schedules are assembled.
source_theorem.relationship: The local library adds measure, kernel, filtration, conditional-law, finite-index, and countable-all-time adapters needed by generated bandit trajectories.

contract.model: A real-valued random variable X on a probability space.
contract.assumptions: X is centered and σ-sub-Gaussian in the moment-generating-function sense; the deviation ε is nonnegative.
contract.parameters: Sub-Gaussian scale σ and deviation threshold ε.
contract.regret: Not a regret theorem; this is a one-sided concentration primitive consumed by later regret proofs.
contract.guarantee: The upper-tail probability is at most exp(-ε²/(2σ²)).

primary.title: Bandit Algorithms
primary.sections: Ch. 6

notation.meaning: the number of exploration pulls allocated to each arm
the empirical mean reward observed from arm a
the regret paid each time suboptimal arm a is selected

steps.title: Explore
steps.detail: Pull every arm m times, usually in round-robin order.

steps.title: Estimate
steps.detail: Compute each arm's empirical mean from its exploration samples.

steps.title: Commit
steps.detail: Choose an empirical maximizer using a documented tie rule.

steps.title: Exploit
steps.detail: Pull that chosen arm for every remaining round.

pseudocode.title: Textbook Explore-Then-Commit
pseudocode.intro: This version makes the exploration budget, commit time, empirical means, and tie convention explicit before the regret theorem is read.
pseudocode.fallback: Average the first m samples of each arm and commit to the least-encoded arm with the largest empirical mean.
lines: input: k arms, horizon n, exploration count m with 1 ≤ m ≤ n/k
for s = 1,…,m: for a = 1,…,k: pull arm a and record X_{a,s}
compute μ̂_a = (1/m) sum_s X_{a,s} for every arm a
set a_hat to the least-encoded empirical-mean maximizer
for every remaining round: pull a_hat and record its reward
pseudocode.relationship: The textbook permits any fixed empirical-mean tie rule. BanditRLlib's canonical generated ETC route fixes round-robin exploration and an explicit first-occurrence/least-encoded commit rule, then proves measurability and expected regret under its bounded or sub-Gaussian arm-law contracts.

worked_example.title: Follow one two-arm explore–then–commit run
worked_example.intro: Take two arms, horizon n = 12, and m = 3 exploration pulls per arm. The six exploration rewards below are deliberately small enough to compute by hand.

steps.title: Explore both arms equally
steps.detail: Round-robin exploration gives each arm three observations before any commitment is made.
steps.fallback: Arm 1 produces rewards 1, 0, 1; arm 2 produces rewards 0, 1, 0 during exploration.

steps.title: Compare the empirical means
steps.detail: Arm 1 has the larger empirical mean, so the documented least-encoded tie rule is not needed in this run.
steps.fallback: The empirical means are two thirds for arm 1 and one third for arm 2, so the committed arm is arm 1.

steps.title: Commit for the remaining rounds
steps.detail: After six exploration pulls, the policy uses arm 1 for the final six rounds. If the true means are 0.6 and 0.4, the exploration of arm 2 has already paid three gap units; a wrong commit would instead repeat that gap throughout exploitation.
steps.fallback: Six rounds remain; with a gap of 0.2, the three exploratory pulls of arm 2 contribute expected pseudo-regret 0.6.

worked_example.takeaway: ETC makes one irreversible decision. Increasing m raises the certain exploration cost but makes the empirical winner more reliable, which is exactly the two-term tradeoff in the theorem card.
worked_example.boundary: The displayed rewards are one illustrative history, not a simulation result. The regret sentence uses hypothetical true means only to explain gap accounting; the source theorem and exact Lean declarations below control the probabilistic assumptions.

source_theorem.label: Theorem 6.1 (ETC regret bound)
source_theorem.fallback: ETC regret is bounded by the exploration cost plus the remaining horizon times exponentially small wrong-commit probabilities.
source_theorem.plain: The theorem exposes the central ETC tradeoff: more exploration costs regret now but reduces the probability of committing to a wrong arm.
source_theorem.relationship: The local canonical route constructs a measurable generated ETC law and states explicit tie semantics before deriving bounded and sub-Gaussian expected-regret endpoints.

contract.model: A finite k-armed stochastic bandit whose centered arm rewards are 1-sub-Gaussian.
contract.assumptions: The exploration length satisfies 1 ≤ m ≤ n/k; each arm is explored m times and empirical-mean ties are broken by a fixed rule.
contract.parameters: Horizon n, arm count k, exploration count m, and gaps Δ_i.
contract.regret: Expected frequentist regret R_n of Explore-Then-Commit.
contract.guarantee: Exploration cost plus the remaining horizon weighted by exponentially small wrong-commit probabilities.

primary.title: Bandit Algorithms
primary.sections: Ch. 7; KL-UCB extension in Ch. 10

notation.meaning: the number of samples collected from arm a before round t
arm a's empirical mean after those samples
the empirical mean plus a confidence bonus; UCB selects a maximal score

steps.title: Initialize
steps.detail: Pull every arm so that each empirical mean and count is defined.

steps.title: Score every arm
steps.detail: Add a confidence bonus to the arm's empirical mean; less data means a wider bonus.

steps.title: Choose optimistically
steps.detail: Pull an arm with maximal upper-confidence score.

steps.title: Update and repeat
steps.detail: Update that arm's count and empirical mean, then recompute scores next round.

steps.title: Read the proof
steps.detail: On the good event, choosing a suboptimal arm forces its count to still be small; sum gap times count to obtain regret.

pseudocode.title: Textbook Algorithm 3: UCB(δ)
pseudocode.intro: This compact form fixes the horizon convention, confidence index, maximizing rule, and update order used in the textbook route.
pseudocode.fallback: At round t, score arm a by its empirical mean before t plus square root of 2 log(1/delta) divided by its previous pull count; choose the least-encoded maximizing arm.
lines: input: k arms, horizon n, confidence δ = 1/n²
for t = 1,…,k: pull arm t; observe X_t; update N_t and μ̂_t
for t = k+1,…,n:
compute every U_a(t) from rewards observed before round t
choose the least-encoded arm in argmax_a U_a(t)
observe its reward; update only that arm's count and empirical mean
pseudocode.relationship: The textbook also describes an unpulled arm as having infinite index; the explicit round-robin prefix realizes the same initialization requirement. BanditRLlib's canonical generated route uses round-robin initialization and a least-encoded maximizer, but its native score is parameterized as √(2c log(t+1)/N_a(t)); the source theorem card and exact Lean declarations remain authoritative for constants and indexing.

proof_bridge.title: Why an optimistic choice becomes a regret bound
proof_bridge.summary: The source proof and the local Lean route use the same four conceptual joints. Read this bridge before comparing constants or implementation details.

steps.title: Control every empirical mean
steps.detail: Work on a confidence event where each empirical mean stays within its declared radius of the true arm mean.
steps.fallback: For every relevant arm and round, the empirical mean error is at most its confidence radius.

steps.title: Use optimism at the selected arm
steps.detail: If a suboptimal arm is chosen on that event, its upper-confidence score must still compete with the optimal arm's mean.
steps.fallback: Selecting a suboptimal arm on the confidence event forces its gap to be no larger than twice its current radius.

steps.title: Turn the radius into a count threshold
steps.detail: Because the radius shrinks with the number of samples, the preceding inequality can hold only while the arm has been pulled comparatively few times.
steps.fallback: The pull count of a suboptimal arm is controlled by a logarithmic term divided by the squared arm gap.

steps.title: Charge every pull by its gap
steps.detail: Apply the pathwise gap-sum identity, then account explicitly for the confidence-event failure probability under the generated trajectory law.
steps.fallback: Expected pseudo-regret is at most the sum of each positive gap times its pull-count bound plus its explicit failure-event charge.

proof_bridge.boundary: This is a reading aid for the shared proof shape. The source theorem card and exact Lean statement below remain authoritative for the model, constants, horizon convention, and confidence schedule.

worked_example.title: Why UCB may deliberately choose the arm with the lower empirical mean
worked_example.intro: Take a two-arm UCB(δ) decision near the end of a horizon n = 20, so δ = 1/n² = 1/400. Before round 20, arm 1 has been sampled 15 times and arm 2 only 4 times.

steps.title: Start from the observed history
steps.detail: Arm 1 currently looks better, but arm 2 is much less explored.
steps.fallback: Arm 1 has count 15 and empirical mean 0.60; arm 2 has count 4 and empirical mean 0.30.

steps.title: Add uncertainty, not just reward
steps.detail: With 2 log(400) approximately 11.98, the under-sampled arm receives the wider confidence bonus.
steps.fallback: The two upper-confidence scores are approximately 1.49 for arm 1 and 2.03 for arm 2.

steps.title: Choose optimism and shrink it with data
steps.detail: UCB selects arm 2 even though its empirical mean is lower. Each additional pull increases N₂, narrows its bonus, and makes persistent suboptimal selection harder to justify.
steps.fallback: At round 20 the policy chooses arm 2 because its upper-confidence score is larger; its bonus decreases as its sample count increases.

worked_example.takeaway: UCB is not greedily choosing the largest empirical mean. It chooses the largest plausible mean, so uncertainty creates exploration and the count-dependent radius eventually limits repeated pulls of a genuinely suboptimal arm.
worked_example.boundary: The numbers illustrate one UCB(δ) decision; they are not a simulated regret result or a new Lean theorem. The source card and compiled declarations below control the exact assumptions and constants.

source_theorem.label: Theorem 7.2 (finite-time UCB regret)
source_theorem.fallback: The textbook UCB policy has a finite-time regret bound with a leading square-root term in horizon, arm count, and log horizon.
source_theorem.plain: Confidence validity implies a suboptimal arm can be selected only while its sample count is small enough to keep its bonus competitive.
source_theorem.relationship: BanditRLlib's ordinary-UCB route uses an explicit generated trajectory and confidence schedule. Its exact hypotheses, constants, gap-sum form, and Tδ failure term are therefore not presented as a line-for-line formalization of Theorem 7.2; KL-UCB remains a separate extension.

contract.model: A finite stochastic k-armed bandit in the textbook's 1-sub-Gaussian environment class.
contract.assumptions: Each arm has a fixed mean and 1-sub-Gaussian noise; the chapter's canonical independent reward-table model supplies the samples used by the proof.
contract.parameters: Algorithm 3, UCB(δ), at horizon n with δ = 1/n²; an unpulled arm has infinite index, otherwise the index is its empirical mean plus √(2 log(1/δ) / count).
contract.regret: The textbook expected regret Rₙ over n rounds.
contract.guarantee: A worst-case finite-time upper bound 8√(nk log n) plus three times the sum of arm gaps.

primary.title: Bandit Algorithms
primary.sections: Ch. 19–20; stopping times in §3.3

companion.title: Improved Algorithms for Linear Stochastic Bandits
companion.authors: Yasin Abbasi-Yadkori, Dávid Pál, and Csaba Szepesvári

notation.meaning: the regularized feature Gram matrix that records explored directions
the ridge least-squares estimate of the unknown reward parameter
the confidence radius multiplying the inverse-Gram feature norm

steps.title: Update geometry
steps.detail: Accumulate the regularized feature Gram matrix from past actions.

steps.title: Estimate
steps.detail: Compute the ridge least-squares parameter estimate.

steps.title: Build confidence
steps.detail: Place plausible parameters in an ellipsoid around the estimate.

steps.title: Act optimistically
steps.detail: Choose the action and plausible parameter pair with the largest predicted reward.

steps.title: Charge widths
steps.detail: Bound regret by confidence widths and use the elliptical-potential sum.

pseudocode.title: OFUL optimistic ridge loop
pseudocode.intro: The compact loop separates the state carried between rounds from the confidence maximization performed at the current round.
pseudocode.fallback: Form the regularized Gram matrix and ridge estimate, then choose the feasible action with the largest estimated reward plus its confidence width.
lines: input: regularization λ > 0, confidence δ, feasible action sets D_t
initialize V_1 = λ I and b_1 = 0
for t = 1,…,n:
set θ̂_t = V_t^{-1} b_t and compute confidence radius β_t
choose a documented maximizer of <θ̂_t,x> + β_t ||x||_{V_t^{-1}}
observe y_t; update V_{t+1} = V_t + x_t x_t^T and b_{t+1} = b_t + x_t y_t
pseudocode.relationship: The source algorithm permits time-varying feasible sets. BanditRLlib's canonical route is a finite-action measurable construction with explicit confidence, all-horizon, expectation, and stopping-time interfaces; the exact Lean statements determine the feature, regularity, and scheduling contracts.

worked_example.title: Why an unexplored direction can beat a better estimate
worked_example.intro: Use two-dimensional features with actions e₁ and e₂, regularization λ = 1, and confidence radius β₂ = 0.5. After one modest reward from e₁, OFUL compares estimated reward and directional uncertainty.

steps.title: Record one observed direction
steps.detail: The first action is e₁ and its reward is 0.2, so only the first coordinate enters the data vector.
steps.fallback: The policy observes reward 0.2 after choosing the first basis vector, so the data vector is (0.2, 0).

steps.title: See uncertainty in the Gram geometry
steps.detail: The observed direction receives an extra rank-one update; the untouched direction retains the larger inverse-Gram width.
steps.fallback: The Gram matrix is diagonal with entries 2 and 1; the estimate is (0.1, 0), and the unexplored second direction has the wider confidence norm.

steps.title: Let optimism choose information
steps.detail: The small estimated advantage of e₁ is outweighed by e₂'s wider confidence interval, so the optimistic score explores e₂.
steps.fallback: The optimistic scores are about 0.454 for the first direction and 0.5 for the unexplored second direction, so OFUL chooses the second direction.

worked_example.takeaway: OFUL explores directions, not named arms in isolation. The same inverse-Gram norm that makes e₂ attractive here is later summed by the elliptical-potential argument.
worked_example.boundary: This two-dimensional calculation illustrates one optimistic score comparison. It is not a trajectory benchmark and does not instantiate every boundedness, measurability, or confidence-radius hypothesis in the compiled theorem.

proof_bridge.title: How confidence geometry pays for linear-bandit regret
proof_bridge.summary: OFUL replaces one confidence interval per arm by one ellipsoid for the unknown parameter. The same inverse-Gram norm measures both uncertainty and the cost charged to the trajectory.

steps.title: Put the parameter in an ellipsoid
steps.detail: A self-normalized concentration result bounds the ridge-estimation error in the geometry accumulated from earlier features.
steps.fallback: The true parameter lies within beta t of the ridge estimate in the Gram-matrix norm.

steps.title: Convert optimism into one width
steps.detail: Maximizing over the confidence set makes the instantaneous regret no larger than a constant multiple of the selected feature's inverse-Gram width.
steps.fallback: One-step regret is controlled by twice the confidence radius times the selected feature's inverse-Gram norm.

steps.title: Sum widths through determinant growth
steps.detail: The elliptical-potential lemma says that repeatedly visiting a direction increases the Gram determinant and prevents that direction from remaining wide forever.
steps.fallback: The sum of clipped squared confidence widths is at most twice the logarithmic growth of the Gram determinant.

steps.title: Finish with Cauchy-Schwarz
steps.detail: Combining the confidence radius with the potential bound yields the familiar dimension-times-square-root-horizon scale, with the source assumptions determining the logarithms and constants.
steps.fallback: Cumulative regret is controlled by the final confidence radius times the square root of horizon and determinant growth, giving dimension times square-root horizon up to logs.

proof_bridge.boundary: This bridge identifies the source proof joints and their local counterparts; it is not a claim that the finite-action Lean route reproduces every OFUL variant or the paper's sharp constants verbatim.

source_theorem.label: Abbasi-Yadkori–Pál–Szepesvári, Theorem 3
source_theorem.math: R_n=\widetilde O\!\left(d\sqrt n\right)\quad\text{under the theorem's bounded-feature and sub-Gaussian assumptions}.
source_theorem.fallback: OFUL achieves dimension times square-root-horizon regret, up to logarithmic factors, under the paper's stated assumptions.
source_theorem.plain: The paper combines a self-normalized confidence ellipsoid with optimism and an elliptical-potential argument.
source_theorem.relationship: The local finite-action scalar route compiles the confidence, optimistic policy, all-time, expected-consistency, and stopping-time interfaces under its own explicit contracts; consult the exact Lean statements for the narrower model.

contract.model: A d-dimensional stochastic linear bandit with round-dependent feasible action sets and linear conditional mean rewards.
contract.assumptions: The paper's preceding bounded-parameter, bounded-feature, conditionally sub-Gaussian noise, and regularization conditions hold; Theorem 3 also assumes every feasible mean reward lies in [-1,1].
contract.parameters: Dimension d, horizon n, feature and parameter bounds, noise scale, regularization λ, and confidence δ.
contract.regret: High-probability cumulative pseudo-regret of the OFUL policy.
contract.guarantee: An explicit confidence-dependent bound of order d√n up to logarithmic factors.

primary.sections: Ch. 34 and Ch. 36

notation.meaning: the posterior distribution after observing the history through round t
a parameter sample drawn from that posterior
an arm optimal for the sampled parameter, with ties handled explicitly

steps.title: Condition
steps.detail: Form the posterior distribution of the unknown environment given observed history.

steps.title: Sample a model
steps.detail: Draw one plausible environment from that posterior.

steps.title: Optimize the sample
steps.detail: Choose an arm that is best in the sampled environment.

steps.title: Observe and update
steps.detail: Record the reward and condition the posterior on the enlarged history.

pseudocode.title: Posterior-sampling loop
pseudocode.intro: This form makes probability matching visible: sample one environment from the current posterior, then act optimally for that sampled environment.
pseudocode.fallback: Sample a latent environment from the posterior given the previous history, then choose the least-encoded arm with maximal mean in that sampled environment.
lines: input: prior Q, likelihood/reward kernel, horizon n, fixed optimal-arm tie rule
initialize posterior Π_1 = Q
for t = 1,…,n:
sample θ̃_t from Π_t given the visible history H_{t-1}
choose A_t as the documented mean-optimal arm for θ̃_t
observe reward X_t and update Π_{t+1} by conditioning on (A_t,X_t)
pseudocode.relationship: BanditRLlib constructs a canonical posterior kernel and a recursive stationary latent-arm-stream trajectory. Its selector carries an explicit pointwise mean-optimality contract, and its compiled endpoint is Bayesian rather than a universal frequentist theorem for every Thompson variant.

worked_example.title: Read one Thompson decision as probability matching
worked_example.intro: After the current history, suppose the posterior says arm 1 is optimal with probability 0.7 and arm 2 with probability 0.3. Thompson sampling turns that uncertainty directly into its next-action law.

steps.title: Start from posterior uncertainty
steps.detail: The probabilities describe uncertainty about the true optimal arm under the Bayesian model, not empirical-mean scores.
steps.fallback: Given the previous history, the posterior probability that arm 1 is optimal is 0.7 and that arm 2 is optimal is 0.3.

steps.title: Sample a plausible environment
steps.detail: If this posterior draw makes arm 2 optimal, the documented selector chooses arm 2 even though arm 1 is more likely to be truly optimal.
steps.fallback: A sampled environment is drawn from the posterior; in this illustrative draw arm 2 is best, so arm 2 is selected.

steps.title: Recover the action probabilities
steps.detail: Across posterior draws, applying the same optimal-arm rule reproduces the posterior law of the true optimal arm.
steps.fallback: Conditioned on the history, Thompson sampling chooses arms 1 and 2 with probabilities 0.7 and 0.3.

worked_example.takeaway: Thompson sampling explores because posterior uncertainty remains: a 30 percent chance that arm 2 is optimal becomes a 30 percent chance of sampling it.
worked_example.boundary: The numbers specify one hypothetical posterior state and do not perform a Bayesian update. The exact compiled route below constructs the posterior kernel and proves probability matching under its stated latent-environment and tie-breaking contracts.

proof_bridge.title: Why posterior sampling can be analyzed through probability matching
proof_bridge.summary: The analysis uses the fact that the action selected from a posterior sample and the truly optimal action have the same conditional distribution given the visible history.

steps.title: Condition on the observed history
steps.detail: Given the current history, both the unknown environment and the fresh posterior sample are distributed according to the same posterior kernel.
steps.fallback: Conditionally on the previous history, the sampled and true latent environments share the current posterior law.

steps.title: Match the optimal-action law
steps.detail: Applying the same documented optimal-arm selector to those two latent environments gives equal conditional laws for the chosen arm and the optimal arm.
steps.fallback: For each arm, its conditional chance of being selected equals its conditional chance of being optimal.

steps.title: Rewrite Bayesian regret
steps.detail: Probability matching permits a clipped upper-confidence decomposition in which uncertainty and failure terms are separated before expectations are summed.
steps.fallback: Conditional Bayesian regret is bounded by an uncertainty term for the selected arm plus an upper-confidence failure term for the optimal arm.

steps.title: Sum uncertainty under the model contract
steps.detail: The bounded-reward, variance, and posterior assumptions then control the accumulated widths and failure charge, producing the source theorem's Bayesian rate.
steps.fallback: Under the stated Bayesian finite-arm assumptions, the accumulated terms yield a constant times square root of k n log n.

proof_bridge.boundary: This is a conceptual map of the Bayesian route. The exact compiled terminal has its own boundedness and variance terms and does not establish a frequentist guarantee for arbitrary Thompson-sampling implementations.

source_theorem.label: Theorem 36.1 (Bayesian regret of Thompson sampling)
source_theorem.math: BR_n\le C\sqrt{kn\log n}\quad\text{for the theorem's Bayesian finite-armed model and universal }C.
source_theorem.fallback: In the stated Bayesian finite-armed setting, Thompson sampling has square-root-horizon Bayesian regret up to a logarithmic factor.
source_theorem.plain: Probability matching turns posterior uncertainty about the best arm into an exploration policy.
source_theorem.relationship: BanditRLlib constructs a canonical posterior/kernel and generated stationary latent-arm-stream process. Its compiled terminal has explicit bounded-reward and variance terms and is not a blanket frequentist guarantee for all Thompson variants.

contract.model: A k-armed Bayesian bandit environment with prior Q and arm laws indexed by the latent environment.
contract.assumptions: For every environment and arm, the centered reward law is 1-sub-Gaussian and its mean lies in [0,1]; optimal-arm ties use the algorithm's fixed rule.
contract.parameters: Prior Q, arm count k, and horizon n.
contract.regret: Bayesian regret BR_n, averaged over the prior, observations, and policy randomization.
contract.guarantee: BR_n is at most C√(kn log n) for a universal constant C.

primary.title: Bandit Algorithms

notation.meaning: the probability of selecting arm a at round t
the importance-weighted loss estimate formed from bandit feedback
the learning rate controlling how aggressively exponential weights move

steps.title: Turn weights into probabilities
steps.detail: Normalize positive arm weights into the current sampling law.

steps.title: Sample an arm
steps.detail: Draw the current action from that probability vector.

steps.title: Estimate all losses
steps.detail: Use the observed loss divided by its sampling probability for the selected arm; use zero for the others.

steps.title: Update exponentially
steps.detail: Downweight arms according to their estimated cumulative losses.

steps.title: Separate guarantees
steps.detail: Expected, fixed-horizon tail, all-time, and sparse-loss results use distinct concentration interfaces.

pseudocode.title: EXP3 importance-weighted update
pseudocode.intro: The loop names the sampling law, the one-coordinate unbiased loss estimate, and the exponential update used by the potential argument.
pseudocode.fallback: Normalize positive weights, sample an arm, divide the observed loss by that arm's probability, and exponentially downweight each arm by its estimated loss.
lines: input: k arms, horizon n, learning rate η; initialize w_1(a) = 1
for t = 1,…,n:
normalize weights into the sampling law p_t
sample A_t ~ p_t and observe only loss ℓ_t(A_t)
set ℓ̂_t(a) = ℓ_t(A_t) 1{A_t=a} / p_t(a) for every arm
update w_{t+1}(a) = w_t(a) exp(-η ℓ̂_t(a))
pseudocode.relationship: The displayed equations are the textbook core. worked_example.title: One EXP3 update from a single observed loss
worked_example.intro: Start with two equal weights, learning rate η = 0.25, and suppose the sampled second arm incurs loss 0.8. The update shows why dividing by the sampling probability is both necessary and noisy.

steps.title: Sample from equal weights
steps.detail: Both arms initially have the same probability; this particular history samples arm 2.
steps.fallback: Both initial weights are one, both probabilities are one half, and arm 2 is sampled with observed loss 0.8.

steps.title: Reconstruct an unbiased loss coordinate
steps.detail: Only arm 2 is observed. Dividing by its probability produces a larger estimate whose conditional expectation equals the hidden loss coordinate.
steps.fallback: The estimated loss is zero for arm 1 and 1.6 for arm 2 because the observed 0.8 is divided by probability one half.

steps.title: Downweight the observed loss
steps.detail: The exponential update lowers arm 2's weight, so arm 1 becomes more likely at the next round without assigning arm 2 zero probability.
steps.fallback: The next weights are approximately 1 and 0.6703, so arm 1 receives probability about 0.599.

worked_example.takeaway: Importance weighting repairs the missing feedback in expectation, while its enlarged squared magnitude creates the variance term that the EXP3 proof must pay for.
worked_example.boundary: This is one deterministic arithmetic trace conditional on a sampled action. It is not an adversarial-regret experiment and does not merge the expected, fixed-window, all-prefix, or realized-regret theorem contracts.

proof_bridge.title: How one bandit observation becomes an adversarial regret guarantee
proof_bridge.summary: EXP3 couples an unbiased importance-weighted estimator with the exponential-weights potential. The proof must pay explicitly for the estimator's second moment.

steps.title: Recover every coordinate in expectation
steps.detail: Although only the selected loss is observed, positive sampling probability makes the importance-weighted estimate conditionally unbiased.
steps.fallback: Given the past, the importance-weighted estimated loss of each arm has expectation equal to that arm's actual loss.

steps.title: Compare exponential potentials
steps.detail: The log change of total weight compares the algorithm's estimated loss with any fixed arm, leaving a learning-rate times second-moment penalty.
steps.fallback: Estimated regret is at most log k over eta plus eta over two times the accumulated estimated-loss second moment.

steps.title: Pay for bandit noise
steps.detail: Importance weighting inflates individual observations, but averaging under the sampling law bounds the conditional second-moment contribution by the number of arms.
steps.fallback: The conditional expected weighted squared estimate is at most the number of arms.

steps.title: Balance the two costs
steps.detail: Choosing the learning rate so that the initial-complexity and variance terms match yields the square-root expected-regret rate.
steps.fallback: With the balanced learning rate, expected regret is at most the square root of two n k log k.

proof_bridge.boundary: The bridge follows the textbook expected-regret argument. BanditRLlib's fixed-window, all-prefix, realized, and sparse-loss extensions have additional hypotheses and are intentionally not collapsed into this one card.

source_theorem.label: Theorem 11.2 (EXP3 expected regret)
source_theorem.fallback: With the textbook learning rate, EXP3 has expected adversarial regret at most the square root of two times horizon, arm count, and log arm count.
source_theorem.plain: Importance weighting makes the bandit observation unbiased, while exponential weights controls the resulting estimated-loss regret.
source_theorem.relationship: The local generated predictable process uses its own tuning constants and also compiles separate fixed-horizon, all-time, realized-regret, and sparse-loss extensions.

pseudocode.title: Half-Tsallis FTRL / Tsallis-INF core
pseudocode.intro: This compact route shows where the regularizer, loss estimator, and round-dependent learning rate meet; estimator-specific corrections remain explicit.
pseudocode.fallback: Choose the simplex distribution minimizing cumulative estimated loss plus the scheduled half-Tsallis regularizer, then form the stated bandit loss estimate from the sampled arm.
lines: input: K arms, half-Tsallis regularizer Ψ_t, schedule η_t, estimator variant
initialize cumulative estimated loss L̂_0 = 0
for t = 1,…,T:
choose p_t by the regularized FTRL minimization over the simplex
sample A_t ~ p_t; observe the selected loss and form the declared estimator ℓ̂_t
set L̂_t = L̂_{t-1} + ℓ̂_t and advance the learning-rate schedule

worked_example.title: See estimator noise and gap credit in one round
worked_example.intro: At one two-arm round, suppose the FTRL distribution is p = (0.25, 0.75), arm 1 is sampled, and its observed loss is 0.5. The arithmetic exposes the two quantities that the regularizer must reconcile.

steps.title: Importance-weight the observed coordinate
steps.detail: Only arm 1 is observed, so its loss is divided by the probability with which it was sampled.
steps.fallback: Arm 1 is sampled with probability 0.25 and loss 0.5, producing estimated loss vector (2, 0).

steps.title: Notice the rare-arm variance cost
steps.detail: A small sampling probability makes the realized estimate large; its conditional second moment carries the inverse-probability geometry.
steps.fallback: The conditional second moment of arm 1's importance-weighted estimate is 0.25 divided by 0.25, which equals 1.

steps.title: Compare the stochastic gap credit
steps.detail: If arm 2 is optimal and arm 1 has mean-loss gap 0.2, the same probability mass contributes a smaller but structured self-bounding term.
steps.fallback: With gap 0.2, sampling arm 1 with probability 0.25 contributes instantaneous expected gap cost 0.05.

worked_example.takeaway: The estimator creates an inverse-probability noise charge, while stochastic gaps price suboptimal probability mass. Half-Tsallis curvature is useful because its stability geometry can connect these two scales.
worked_example.boundary: This is a one-round calculation, not a derivation of Tsallis-INF or a compiled general curvature-noise-gap calculus. The theorem cards below remain authoritative for schedules, estimators, constants, and regimes.

proof_bridge.title: Where curvature, estimator noise, and stochastic gaps meet
proof_bridge.summary: Tsallis-INF is useful as a reading lens because its guarantee is assembled from three interacting ingredients rather than from the regularizer alone.

steps.title: Let curvature control stability
steps.detail: Schematically, the FTRL regularizer determines how much the chosen distribution can move when one more estimated loss vector is added.
steps.fallback: One-step FTRL stability is controlled by the regularizer's local inverse curvature.

steps.title: Match curvature to bandit noise
steps.detail: The estimator contributes probability-dependent variance, so the useful curvature is the one that absorbs the same rare-arm geometry.
steps.fallback: The estimated loss second moment grows like the squared loss divided by the arm's sampling probability.

steps.title: Add stochastic self-bounding when available
steps.detail: In an IID gap model, expected regret also lower-bounds the probability mass assigned to suboptimal arms; this can repay part of the stability cost.
steps.fallback: Stochastic regret equals the sum over rounds and suboptimal arms of gap times expected sampling probability.

steps.title: Choose the regime-specific consumer
steps.detail: The adversarial analysis keeps the stability charge, while stochastic, corrupted, drifting, and restart results add distinct assumptions to sharpen or reorganize it.
steps.math: \begin{gathered}\mathcal C+\mathcal V-\mathcal G\Longrightarrow Reg_T\text{ bound},\\ \mathcal C=\text{curvature},\quad\mathcal V=\text{noise},\quad\mathcal G=\text{gap credit}.\end{gathered}
steps.fallback: Curvature, estimator noise, and a stated self-bounding or drift contract combine only within a particular regret theorem.

proof_bridge.boundary: This motif is a teaching organization of existing proof routes, not a compiled general curvature-noise-gap calculus. The source theorem cards and each Lean declaration remain authoritative for which coupling has actually been proved.

source_theorem.label: Zimmert–Seldin, Theorem 1 (adversarial regime)
source_theorem.fallback: The source theorem gives explicit adversarial square-root regret bounds for importance-weighted and reduced-variance Tsallis-INF variants.
source_theorem.plain: The half-Tsallis regularizer is designed to retain adversarial robustness while adapting sharply to stochastic self-bounding structure.
source_theorem.relationship: BanditRLlib proves a scheduled half-Tsallis route and several IID, corrupted, drifting, and oracle-restart consumers. These are source-aligned local theorems, not a claim that every sharp paper regime has been reproduced verbatim.

the stage-h action value used by backward planning

steps.title: Count strict prefixes
steps.detail: Before episode k, aggregate visits and next-state transitions from episodes strictly earlier than k.

steps.title: Estimate transitions
steps.detail: Normalize transition counts at each state-action pair, with an explicit zero-count convention.

steps.title: Plan backward optimistically
steps.detail: Add a Hoeffding bonus, clip against the horizon and previous Q table, and run backward dynamic programming.

steps.title: Execute the greedy policy
steps.detail: Generate the next episode with the measurable greedy policy from that recurrent table.

steps.title: Assemble regret
steps.detail: Combine confidence and optimism with charge, Bellman-innovation, and low-count bounds on the same process.

pseudocode.title: Known-reward UCBVI-CH episode loop
pseudocode.intro: The episode-level pseudocode fixes strict-prefix counts, backward stage order, previous-Q clipping, the greedy policy, and the generated-trajectory update.
pseudocode.fallback: At each stage of episode k, clip the reward plus empirical next value plus bonus by the remaining horizon and the previous Q table, then take the maximum over actions.
lines: input: finite MDP, known rewards, horizon H, episodes K, confidence δ
initialize optimistic Q_{0,h}; keep zero-count transition and tie rules explicit
for episode k = 1,…,K: aggregate visits/transitions from episodes < k
set V_{k,H+1} = 0; for h = H,…,1 compute every clipped Q_{k,h}(s,a)
set π_{k,h}(s) to the documented maximizer of Q_{k,h}(s,·)
execute π_k for one episode; append states and actions to the recurrent history
pseudocode.relationship: The source paper contains both CH and Bernstein variants. BanditRLlib's compiled canonical endpoint is the known-deterministic-reward Hoeffding UCBVI-CH route on one recurrent generated process, with strict-prefix counts, a documented tie rule, the frozen 20/250 bound, and a separate expected consumer.

worked_example.title: One optimistic Bellman backup in a tiny MDP
worked_example.intro: Consider stage h = 1 of a two-stage episode at state s. Two actions have empirical next-stage values 0.5 and 0.2; the second action has been visited only once, so its Hoeffding bonus is much larger.

steps.title: Read only earlier episodes
steps.detail: Strict-prefix counting prevents the current episode from leaking into its own policy. The rarely visited action carries less transition evidence.
steps.fallback: Before episode k, the safe action has ten visits and the new action has one visit at this state and stage.

steps.title: Add the transition bonuses
steps.detail: With zero immediate reward and nonbinding clips, the optimistic backup can prefer the uncertain action even though its empirical next value is lower.
steps.fallback: The safe action's optimistic value is 0.6, while the under-sampled action's optimistic value is 0.8.

steps.title: Execute, then narrow the next episode
steps.detail: The greedy policy tries the new action. If later data leave its empirical value near 0.2 while its bonus falls to 0.2, its score drops below the safe action's 0.6.
steps.fallback: Episode k chooses the new action; after its bonus falls to 0.2, its illustrative score becomes 0.4 and no longer beats 0.6.

worked_example.takeaway: UCBVI performs UCB inside backward dynamic programming. Counts control local transition uncertainty, while the proof must propagate optimism and charge those bonuses along the same generated episodic trajectory.
worked_example.boundary: The values and bonuses are illustrative and keep clipping inactive for readability. They are not a simulation, do not specify a full transition kernel, and do not claim the Bernstein or unknown-reward variants.

proof_bridge.title: How local transition confidence becomes episodic regret
proof_bridge.summary: UCBVI repeats the optimism pattern inside dynamic programming. Concentration is local to state-action-stage counts, while the final regret statement is global across a generated sequence of episodes.

steps.title: Control empirical transitions
steps.detail: For every visited state-action-stage tuple, a confidence event bounds the error of applying the empirical transition kernel to a bounded next-value function.
steps.fallback: The empirical-transition prediction error for the next value is no larger than its exploration bonus.

steps.title: Propagate optimism backward
steps.detail: Backward induction shows that adding the bonus and clipping at the remaining horizon keeps the recurrent Q table above the optimal value on the good event.
steps.fallback: On the confidence event, the optimistic episode-k Q value dominates the optimal Q value at every stage.

steps.title: Decompose one episode
steps.detail: Optimism turns policy-value regret into a sum of bonuses, transition-estimation errors, and a martingale innovation along the executed trajectory.
steps.fallback: The regret of one episode is bounded by the sum of its confidence bonuses, transition errors, and martingale innovations.

steps.title: Charge visits on the same process
steps.detail: Strict-prefix counts control how often large bonuses occur; concentration controls the innovation sum, producing the frozen high-probability CH bound.
steps.fallback: The cumulative regret is bounded by the explicit 20 times square-root term plus the 250 times lower-order term.

proof_bridge.boundary: This bridge is for the known-reward Hoeffding UCBVI-CH route. It does not silently import the Bernstein variant, unknown-reward extensions, or a different trajectory process.

source_theorem.label: Azar–Osband–Munos, Theorem 1 (UCBVI-CH)
source_theorem.fallback: With high probability, UCBVI-CH regret is bounded by a 20-times square-root leading term plus the explicit 250-times lower-order term.
source_theorem.plain: The UCBVI-CH analysis couples empirical-transition concentration, backward optimism, cumulative bonuses, and a martingale innovation term.
source_theorem.relationship: The compiled local endpoint is deliberately narrow: finite horizon, known deterministic rewards, the same recurrent generated process, strict-prefix counts, policy-value pseudo-regret, the frozen 20/250 high-probability bound, and an expected consumer with an additional KHδ failure term.

contract.model: An episodic finite MDP with S states, A actions, horizon H, K episodes, and total time T = KH.
contract.assumptions: State and action sets are finite; rewards are known, deterministic, and in [0,1]; transitions are stationary and unknown; the paper's MDP regularity assumption holds.
contract.parameters: S, A, H, K, confidence δ, and L = log(5HSAT/δ).
contract.regret: Cumulative policy-value regret across the first K episodes.
contract.guarantee: With probability at least 1-δ, regret is bounded by the displayed 20/250 UCBVI-CH expression.

source_theorems.label: Chapter2 prescient dependency: real nonsmooth minimizer comparison
source_theorems.plain: E is a real normed vector space; V is a subset, p belongs toV, and f:E->R is convex onV (including convexity ofV). The supplied p actually minimizes f+h overV. Only h has a specified ambient continuous Frechet derivative atp. No derivative or continuity of f, convexity of h, completeness/inner product/finite dimension, or closed/open/bounded/coercive V is assumed. EmptyV is ruled out by p membership; boundary/singleton/lower-dimensional sets and u=p are allowed. Every comparator u belongs to the sameV. Fix u inV and put q(a)=p+a(u-p),0<=a<=1. Feasibility follows from convexity ofV. Actual minimality and convexity of f give f(p)+h(p)<=f(q(a))+h(q(a))<=(1-a)f(p)+a f(u)+h(q(a)). Hence H(a)=a(f(u)-f(p))+h(q(a))-h(p)>=0=H(0). Differentiate only h along the affine segment: Hprime(0)=f(u)-f(p)+Dh(p)[u-p]. At a minimum on[0,1], the positive tangent direction1 gives Hprime(0)>=0. Rearranging yields f(p)-f(u)<=Dh(p)[u-p]. This proves the loss comparison from an actual minimum, without a supplied regret/stability bound or differentiability of the loss.

source_theorems.label: Chapter 2 prescient dependency: extended losses on a finite feasible domain
source_theorems.plain: The same EReal loss f, convex feasible set V and canonical ordered divergence Bψ(a;b)=ψ(a)−ψ(b)−Dψ(b)[a−b] are used throughout. Properness excludes negative infinity everywhere and supplies one finite point. At every feasible z, a source subgradient supports f at every ambient y. This global support condition implies that f is finite at every point of V; outside V, positive infinity is allowed. The first bridge uses an arbitrary real inner-product space. The other two explicitly retain completeness from the reused minimum-order API. Finite Euclidean source spaces are covered; minimal assumptions are not claimed. The result is convexity of z ↦ (f z).toReal restricted to V. Taking toReal at infinity gives zero, so the total real function need not be globally convex. The proof selects a global support at the feasible convex combination, compares the two feasible endpoints, and cancels the weighted inner products after feasible finiteness has been established. For a supplied p in V and finite f on V, the actual EReal objective f(z)+η⁻¹ Bψ(z;x) has a minimum at p exactly when its real finite-part objective does. This order equivalence permits every real η, including zero and negative values, with Lean’s total inverse. It needs no convexity, derivative, positive step size or attainment premise beyond the supplied minimum in each direction. The center x may be outside V and the loss domain. The proof reuses the shared minOn_finitePart_iff on the actual penalized objective. For the one-step comparison, η is positive, V is convex, f is proper and has global supports at every feasible point, p belongs to V and actually minimizes the EReal penalized objective there. The generator ψ has actual ambient derivatives at both x and p. Every u in the same V satisfies η((f p).toReal−(f u).toReal) ≤ Bψ(u;x)−Bψ(u;p)−Bψ(p;x). Both negative residuals and their target/base order are retained. No infinity subtraction, loss derivative, convexity of ψ, closedness of V, bounded domain or existence of minimizers is asserted. Dropping residuals requires separate nonnegativity hypotheses.

worked_example.title: Two rounds with an active projection
worked_example.intro: Use V=[0,1], x1=0, eta=1 and losses -2x followed by x/2. This is the exact public Lean canary.

steps.title: Project the first gradient step
steps.detail: The first gradient is -2. The unconstrained next point is 2, so projection changes it to 1.

steps.title: Use the changed current loss
steps.detail: The second gradient is one half. Its update stays inside the interval.
steps.fallback: The terminal point is one half.

steps.title: Keep a nonzero residual
steps.detail: Against comparator zero, regret and terminal squared distance are both positive.
steps.fallback: Regret is one half and terminal squared distance is one quarter.

source_theorems.label: Ambient completed information gives real causal versions
source_theorems.math: \begin{aligned}\overline{F}^{\mu}&=\{A:\exists B\in F,\ A=_{\mu\text{-AE}}B\},\\P\text{ measurable on }\overline{F}^{\mu}&\Longrightarrow\exists Q\text{ measurable on }F,\\&P=Q\quad\mu\text{-AE},\\F_t\subseteq\sigma(S,Y_{<t}),\ P_t\in[0,1]\text{ AE}&\Longrightarrow\\&P_t=\pi_t(S,Y_{<t})\quad\text{AE for all }t,\\R_T^{\mathrm{expected\ fixed}}&=\sum_{t<T}\mathbb E(P_t-\mathbb EY_0)^2\ge0.\end{aligned}
source_theorems.plain: Embed real values measurably and injectively into countably many Bool coordinates. For each coordinate, augmented measurability supplies an F-measurable representative set with ambient-mu AE equality. Its membership bits form an F-measurable code. Countable intersection makes this code equal the original real code on one full-measure event. The measurable left inverse, extended to every code, produces an actual real F-measurable version equal to the original AE. The embedding is of the real output, so Omega requires no countability or standard-Borel assumption. Apply the actual real-version producer at each natural time, obtain relative AE strong measurability, and reuse the strict-past factorization/clipping producer. Original predictions are AE in[0,1] at every time; clipping gives global feasibility on every seed/history input. One countable intersection gives one AE event for all natural times and one family before all horizons. Obtain a relative measurable version from the completed-field hypothesis. Use the actual private-seed/strict-past independence producer and AE congruence. Joint target independence and seed independence of the WHOLE infinite stream derive independence of the ORIGINAL prediction and current target. No support, same-law, boundedness or prediction-integrability assumption is needed in this independence terminal. Actual completed-information versions supply the accepted AE producer, which derives current independence and bounded L2. The population mean attains minimum EXPECTED fixed unit-comparator loss outside expectation. The common target variance cancels in cumulative expected loss, leaving the sum of original squared deviations. Original predictions appear on both sides, the same infinite process is used for all natural horizons, and T0 is an empty identity. The population mean is analysis-only; no convergence, rate, pathwise or high-probability statement follows.

source_theorems.label: Causal realization of behavioral decision kernels
source_theorems.plain: Apply pinned Mathlib kernel randomization at every natural time and choose one jointly measurable sampler family before any observation law or horizon. Every history has the exact uniform pushforward law. Induct on the actual finite action recursion. Each step restricts both prefixes, generates prior actions and appends the current sample. Prove finite-input measurability, equality of every earlier action with the same infinite process, and pointwise nonanticipation. Independent infinite uniform coordinates give independence of the current draw from the strict past tape. The product law separates the entire observation stream from the tape. Regroup these blocks and map through the actual generated history, then through the sampler; the joint law is history marginal composed with the given kernel. Use the actual measurable generated prediction and established joint law. Conditional-distribution uniqueness identifies the kernel AE under the actual generated-history marginal, including time0. Select one sampler family first and retain its recursion, joint and conditional laws for every observation law. Under coordinate IID, same-law and AE unit observations, lift those assumptions through the product law. The concrete feasible history policy instantiates the existing IID expected-fixed excess producer at every natural horizon, including zero.

source_theorems.label: Actual FTL regret and ordinary-limit semantics
source_theorems.plain: Let Phi_T be the squared loss of the horizon empirical mean. The actual old leader minimizes the prefix of lengthT. Therefore Phi_(T+1) is at most Phi_T plus the actual next loss. Induct from the empty prefix to obtain Phi_T <= the actual FTL cumulative loss, without a supplied regret premise. Use the proved empirical-mean decomposition for positiveT, and empty sums forT0. Subtract that comparator loss from the same actual cumulative FTL loss. The minus T times squared-distance term is retained exactly. Identify the feasible interval minimum with the produced empirical mean. The actual FTL gap is nonnegative by the first endpoint and at most4+4logT by the source theorem. Divide by positiveT and squeeze between zero and a bound tending to zero. For positiveT, divide the exact comparator identity byT: normalized fixed regret equals normalized best regret minus squared distance from the empirical mean. The best term tends to zero. Subtract limits in both directions to obtain the ordinary-limit equivalence. Assume the empirical mean converges to m explicitly. Continuity gives squared-distance convergence to (u-m)^2 for every fixed realu. The exact equivalence gives fixed regret limit -(u-m)^2. This is nonpositive, so restricting comparators to[0,1] supplies the literal ordinary-limit predicate.

The explicit recursion is d0=0 and d(n+1)=1-d(floor(n/2)). Strong induction on the strictly smaller parent produces binary values and hence unit support at every index. Pair the two children of every binary-tree parent to derive S(2n+1)=2n-2S(n). Induction yields S(4^n-1)=2(4^n-1)/3 and the corresponding low-prefix count. algorithm.title: Prove both directions of the maximum rule

steps.title: Lift active supports
steps.detail: An attaining component has fi(x)=F(x) and fi(y)≤F(y) for every ambient y. Its full global support therefore supports F. The maximum support set is convex at this finite query, so the ordinary active convex hull supports F. The active lifting result needs no properness/convexity/continuity; hull-forward needs properness/common finite query but not convexity of the fi or continuity. Those weaker-premise foundations are not the full numbered source terminal.

steps.title: Establish ordinary hull compactness
steps.detail: Ambient continuity and finite query values give actual interior neighborhoods of the effective domains. Shared local support boundedness and closed global inequalities make component supports compact. A convex join is the continuous image of [0,1] times two compact sets; finite induction gives compactness of the ordinary active hull, with inactive sets empty. The generic finite-convex-union helper permits an empty selected Finset; the domain-interior continuity helper permits a bottom query value, unlike the source terminal.

steps.title: Construct the reverse
steps.detail: For g supporting F and EACH direction d, use yn=x+d/(n+1), choose actual maximizing indices and actual component supports at sufficiently large n, and use the finite family local bounds for a compact subsequence. One finite index recurs; the restricted frequent-index filter is NeBot. Continuity makes that index active at x, and the global support limit yields k in its full support set. Actual displacement comparison gives inner(g,d)≤inner(k,d). This k depends on d, including d=0; no single k for all directions and no supplied witness is claimed. If g were outside the ordinary active hull, its compactness and convexity give strict separation by a continuous linear functional. Riesz supplies the corresponding direction d. The constructed active k has at least the directional value of g, contradicting separation. Thus every maximum support belongs to the ordinary hull; both equality directions are proved without a closure replacement.

notation.meaning: At zero-based time t, p receives t whole past losses, t+1 actual outputs, and the current whole loss. The next output is not an input. Policy and initialization are fixed exogenous parameters.

LegalFeedback requires the actual selected vector to be a true global support at every played query. An optional OracleLaw supplies this premise everywhere, but the performance statements do not require off-path legal choices.

Finite-dimensional real inner-product space; shared nonempty closed convex V. Proper EReal losses exclude bottom and have an ambient finite witness; global supports are nonempty at feasible points. Properness and actual supports justify finite toReal loss differences. Only played support membership enters performance. Fixed eta>0 allows T=0 and unbounded V. Variable steps need T>0 and positive nonincreasing played steps with pairwise diameter control. Tuning needs D,G,T>0 and actual selected-norm bounds on the same horizon-prescribed trajectory. Prefix comparisons hold the policy and initialization fixed; they do not impose independence on external parameters.

lines: Fix the shared nonempty closed convex V, feasible x1 and one exogenous policy p.

notation.meaning: Finite-dimensional real WHOLE SPACE only; uniform positive c, old x=c*y and transformed loss f(c*y), initial/comparator divided by c, eta/c^2, selected c*g. Conditional additive dimension-exponent consistency gives eta unit [x]^2/[loss] and regret unit [loss]; this is not a physical-unit type checker or numerical performance theorem. Loss units remain unchanged. No arbitrary constrained-domain projection, anisotropic/affine coordinate or independent choice-function equivariance theorem.

The SAME exogenous deterministic finite-history policy is explicitly adapted: inverse-transform past/current whole losses, multiply played history by c, query original policy, multiply selected answer by c. It receives finite past loss functions/played outputs/current whole loss; exogenous parameter selection itself is not restricted by this function type. ALL natural-round history/output/selected correspondences are derived from the actual shared whole-space nearest-projection recurrence. Arbitrary schedules/structural identities need no positive eta or legal policy; performance requires its separate premises.

Proper means no bottom anywhere and some finite real value. A proper loss/global EReal support at c*y yields a scaled global support; this is a one-way implication, not exact subdifferential-set equality. Prefix properness plus actual old on-path legality produce actual scaled legality, with no off-path oracle law. Bare EReal.toReal regret equality for unrestricted losses is total algebra, not a finite-loss guarantee. The sharp fixed-positive-step theorem requires whole-space SubdifferentiableOn losses and actual legal played supports, which ensure finite played/comparator values; it retains the SAME original-run negative terminal squared-distance residual. The two real gradient-chainrule helpers allow ANY real c under their HasGradientAt/DifferentiableAt hypotheses; invertible loss/path transport requires c>0. c0 inverse identity is inadmissible and fails in the named example; c1 is identity. The fixed eta>0 sharp endpoint includes T0 with exact cancellation. Source known-horizon1/sqrtT requires natural T>=1, and totalized1/sqrt0=0 is not a positive tuned schedule. No anytime, future-informed energy optimizer or minimax/lower-bound certificate.
